## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Health data has a **place**: a village, a block, a facility, a patient's home
- Today: how R stores places, and how to make an **honest map**
- By the end you can:
  - read spatial data and say what an `sf` object is
  - name the **CRS** and **transform** before measuring
  - **join** attributes and **spatially** join points to polygons
  - map **rates, not counts**, with a defensible classification
:::

## Our data: a synthetic district

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **79 blocks** (polygons) with population, poverty, literacy, dengue cases
- **30 health facilities** (points)
- Everything is **invented**: no real boundaries or people
- Built so dengue **clusters** in space: later sessions test that
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = district), colour = "white") + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = NULL) + theme_void(base_size = 16) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
:::

# Topic 1 — Spatial data in R {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Three kinds of vector geometry (plus raster)

| Type | Example | Class |
|---|---|---|
| **Point** | facility, case home | `POINT` |
| **Line** | road, river | `LINESTRING` |
| **Polygon** | block, district | `POLYGON` |
| Raster | population grid, satellite | `terra` / `stars` (not today) |

::: {.key}
An **`sf` object is a data frame with one extra column, `geometry`**. Every `dplyr` verb you know still works.
:::

## Reading a layer

```{r}
class(blocks)
blocks |> st_drop_geometry() |> head(4)
```

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(fill = "grey95", colour = "grey40") + labs(title = "79 blocks")
```

# Topic 2 — Coordinate reference systems {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## A CRS says how numbers become places

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Geographic** (e.g. EPSG:**4326**)

- longitude / latitude in **degrees**
- good for storing and web maps
- **wrong for area and distance**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Projected** (e.g. UTM 44N, EPSG:**32644**)

- **metres**
- good for **area, length, distance, buffers**
- one projection suits one region
:::
:::

```{r}
st_crs(blocks)$input
blocks_utm <- st_transform(blocks, 32644)
st_crs(blocks_utm)$input
```

## Why it matters

```{r}
tibble(block = blocks$block_id[1:3], recorded_km2 = blocks$area_km2[1:3],
       computed_in_metres = round(as.numeric(st_area(blocks_utm))[1:3] / 1e6, 1))
```

::: {.warn}
Always check `st_crs()` before measuring. Two layers can only be combined if they share a CRS, so `st_transform()` one to match the other.
:::

# Topic 3 — Joins {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Attribute join and spatial join

```{r}
fac <- read_csv(fac_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |> st_as_sf(coords = c("easting_m", "northing_m"), crs = 32644)
blocks_utm$n_fac <- lengths(st_intersects(blocks_utm, fac))     # facilities per block
table(blocks_utm$n_fac)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Attribute join:** `left_join(sf_object, table, by = "key")`: same as ordinary data
- **Spatial join:** `st_join(points, polygons)`: *which polygon is each point in?*
- `st_intersects()` / `st_within()` give TRUE/FALSE per pair; `lengths()` counts them
- `st_distance()` gives distances in the CRS units (**metres** if projected)
:::

## Distance to the nearest facility

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
cen <- st_centroid(blocks_utm)
blocks_utm$km_to_fac <- apply(st_distance(cen, fac), 1, min) / 1000
ggplot(blocks_utm) + geom_sf(aes(fill = km_to_fac)) + geom_sf(data = fac, colour = "red", size = 1.6) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "km", direction = -1) + labs(title = "Distance to nearest facility (red = facilities)")
```

# Topic 4 — Honest choropleths {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Counts mislead, rates do not

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-width: 11
p1 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_cases)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Cases") + labs(title = "Counts")
p2 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "per 100,000", option = "magma", direction = -1) + labs(title = "Rate per 100,000")
p1 + p2
```

::: {.key}
Counts follow **population size**. Map **rates** for risk; counts only for workload.
:::

## Classification changes the story

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-width: 11
library(classInt)
cls <- function(x, style) cut(x, classIntervals(x, 5, style = style)$brks, include.lowest = TRUE)
bind_rows(mutate(blocks, scheme = "Equal interval", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "equal")),
          mutate(blocks, scheme = "Quantile", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "quantile")),
          mutate(blocks, scheme = "Jenks", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "jenks"))) |>
  ggplot() + geom_sf(aes(fill = k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + facet_wrap(~ scheme) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlOrRd", name = NULL) + theme_void(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Equal interval:** honest about scale, but a skewed variable crowds one class
- **Quantile:** always shows a "worst 20%" even if all areas are similar
- **Jenks:** groups similar values, but breaks change with the data
- **State the scheme and breaks**; keep them fixed to compare maps
:::

## Colour

::: {.incremental}
- **Sequential** (light to dark) for rates
- **Diverging** only around a meaningful midpoint (e.g. rate ratio = 1)
- No rainbow; `viridis` and ColorBrewer are colour-blind safe
- A good map has a **title, legend with units, source** (and scale bar / north arrow when area matters)
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s1q1", "Why must a layer be transformed to a projected CRS before you call st_area() or st_distance()?",
         c("The functions will not run on a layer that is stored in degrees",
           "Projected systems store more digits, so the answers are more precise",
           "A degree covers a different ground distance at different latitudes",
           "Distances in metres are needed only when you want to draw a map"), answer = 3,
         explain = "A degree of longitude covers a different ground distance at different latitudes, so areas and distances computed in degrees are not meaningful. A projected CRS uses metres.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s1q2", "A district map shows dengue CASES by block, and the largest blocks look worst. What is the best fix?",
         c("Switch to a darker colour scale so that the differences stand out more clearly",
           "Map cases per 100,000 people so different block sizes compare fairly",
           "Remove the blocks that have the largest populations from the map entirely",
           "Use quantile classes so that the very worst blocks are not shown at all"), answer = 2,
         explain = "Counts reflect how many people live in a block. A rate divides by population, which makes risk comparable across blocks.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s1q3", "You have a table of facilities with columns easting_m and northing_m, in UTM zone 44N. What must you give st_as_sf() besides the coordinate columns?",
         c("The number of facilities, to allocate the geometry column",
           "A polygon layer, because points need an area to sit in",
           "The CRS, so R knows how the numbers map to places",
           "Nothing else, since R can guess the system from the numbers"), answer = 3,
         explain = "Coordinates are only numbers until you say which CRS they belong to. Without a CRS you cannot transform them or combine them with other layers.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s1q4", "Which statement about classification of a choropleth is correct?",
         c("Equal-interval classes put the same number of areas in each class",
           "Natural breaks give identical classes whichever data are being mapped",
           "The scheme that is chosen has no influence on how the map pattern looks",
           "Quantile classes show a worst group, even if all areas are similar"), answer = 4,
         explain = "Quantile breaks force equal counts per class, so there is always a top group. Equal intervals do not equalise counts, and every scheme changes the look of the map.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s1q5", "What does st_join(points, polygons) return?",
         c("The points, each with the attributes of the polygon it falls in",
           "The polygons, each with a count of the points that fall inside them",
           "A single geometry made by merging all of the points and polygons",
           "The distances between each point and each one of the polygons"), answer = 1,
         explain = "A spatial join attaches the attributes of the polygon that contains (or intersects) each point to the point rows. Counting points per polygon needs st_intersects() and lengths().")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- An **`sf` object** = data frame + `geometry`
- **Check `st_crs()`**; transform to a projected CRS to measure
- **Attribute joins** use keys; **spatial joins** use location
- **Map rates**; state the **classification**; use sequential colour
:::
